critic.issues: The prompt defines a non-standard 'completion rate' metric (completers / planned enrollment) that is not a pre-specified threshold in the registered protocol — there is no mention of an '≥80% completion rate threshold' anywhere in the context or evidence. The prompt invents this threshold and convention. Additionally, the calculation is straightforward arithmetic from numbers given in the evidence (62+60=122 completers, 122/124=98.4%), making this a trivial computation rather than a genuine forecast. The context already contains the participant flow data (68 started, 62 completed; 66 started, 60 completed) needed to answer the question directly, so no forecasting expertise is required. The 'planned enrollment of 124' is stated in the protocol description in the context. The answer is fully derivable from the context without any predictive reasoning.
critic.calculation: Planned enrollment = 124 (as stated in registered protocol). Completers = 62 + 60 = 122. Completion rate = 122/124 = 98.4%. Threshold is ≥80%. 98.4% ≥ 80%, so yes it met the threshold.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT04992611 (STEAM study), a behavioral factorial RCT comparing circadian-aligned versus circadian-misaligned sleep extension in adolescents, with two co-primary outcomes (overall caloric intake and glycemic load), did the primary outcome statistically favor the circadian-aligned sleep extension arm over the circadian-misaligned arm (i.e., was the direction of the primary endpoint result — lower caloric intake or lower glycemic load in the aligned arm — in the pre-specified beneficial direction for the intervention)? Convention: primary outcome favors intervention means the direction of the primary endpoint result is in the pre-specified beneficial direction for the intervention arm as reported in the posted results table. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
derivation: For caloric intake: aligned arm mean during healthy sleep = lower than misaligned (net mean difference -126.4 kcal, aligned lower). For glycemic load: aligned arm healthy sleep mean 210.4 vs misaligned 170.8 — misaligned is actually lower, so glycemic load does NOT favor aligned. However, the caloric intake primary outcome does favor aligned (negative mean difference = aligned arm lower). The pre-specified hypothesis was that aligned extension would reduce caloric intake relative to misaligned, and the direction for caloric intake is consistent with this. Mixed picture but caloric intake (first primary) directionally favors intervention.
why_hard: Requires reading the direction of the mean difference for each co-primary outcome and reconciling a mixed directional result across the two co-primaries, distinguishing which direction is 'beneficial' for the aligned arm.

Study Overview
Brief Summary
There is strong reason to believe that sleep promotion during adolescence could yield long-term health rewards; the investigators' data show that, when they get more sleep, Morning Larks have impressively reduced intake of overall calories and foods high in glycemic load that are linked to long-term health risk. Before that can be translated into major public health interventions, however, the field needs to understand why similar changes in sleep had no effect, or even an adverse effect, on adolescent Night Owls. This experimental study will clarify why there have been such discrepant effects across Morning Larks and Night Owls, with the goal of more broadly harnessing the promise of improved sleep in the prevention of obesity and long-term morbidity.
Detailed Description
Recent research shows that sleep could play a novel role in preventing obesity and long-term morbidity. Population studies find that too little sleep predicts the development of obesity and experimental studies show that short sleep increases dietary intake without increasing physical activity. Sleep may be a particularly potent intervention target for adolescents. During adolescence, inadequate sleep is very common, obesity rates are rising most, non-sleep-oriented obesity prevention programs have had least success, and young people can develop enduring dietary patterns that set the stage for life-long obesity and health risk. The investigators' lab has shown both the promise of longer sleep for adolescents and a critical knowledge gap. That lab found that extending adolescents' sleep via earlier bedtimes impressively reduced caloric intake for early chronotypes ("Morning Larks"; who prefer early bed- and rise times), but not late chronotypes ("Night Owls"; who prefer late bed- and rise times). The effect was not only statistically strong, but at roughly 400 calories difference per day, could add up to major shifts in body weight over time. Beyond calorie counts, there was a similar discrepancy in the glycemic load consumed by Larks and Owls after sleep extension, and glycemic load has been independently linked to long-term morbidity. The investigators assert that the discrepancy in how Larks and Owls responded to longer sleep is due to circadian misalignment: a mismatch between the timing of external sleep-wake demands and internal biological clock. They investigators propose that, for adolescent Owls, an early-to-bed intervention induces misaligned sleep timing that counters the benefits of longer sleep duration. In adults, severe circadian misalignment dramatically increases the risk for obesity, and even modest misalignment is linked to higher caloric intake. If a cause-effect relationship holds in adolescence, common sleep advice emphasizing earlier bedtimes might waste limited resources or even do harm for Owls. In contrast, an approach that considers chronotype might capitalize on the potent effect of improved sleep that has been shown for Larks. The current protocol reflects a novel experimental study in which 124 healthy 14-18-year-olds (62 Owls and 62 Larks) complete a 3-week trial involving periods of sleep restriction and sleep extension, in which the extension periods are randomly assigned to be aligned vs. misaligned relative to chronotype. Focusing independently on caloric intake and glycemic load, investigators will assess the dietary effect of sleep extension when it is well-timed versus poorly-timed relative to adolescents' internal clocks. The study will test a causal model in which sleep timing plays an important role in promoting or negating the benefits of sleep extension.

Trained interviewers will engage adolescents in 30-min interviews regarding food consumption over the previous 24-hr periods. Description	

The primary outcome for Aim 2 is the averaged daily glycemic load of foods consumed per day during the sleep extension condition, based on the same dietary recall interview procedures described above. Daily Glycemic Load is a "unitless" derived score that allows one to index how much the consumed food induces large swings in blood sugar, which an independent risk factor for chronic health condition. Calculation involves several steps:

Each food is first characterized by a predetermined glycemic index, which is a 0-100 value that represents how fast and far it raises blood sugar.
For each consumed food, glycemic load (GL) is the product of its glycemic index multiplied by the grams of available carbohydrate consumed by the participant, divided by 100.
Total daily GL is the sum of glycemic load values across all foods consumed during a given day.
Finally, for this primary outcome measure, we averaged the total daily GL across assessed days within a sleep condition.

critic.issues: The prompt asks whether the primary outcome 'statistically favored' the aligned arm, but then clarifies 'direction of the primary endpoint result in the pre-specified beneficial direction.' This conflates statistical significance with directional favorability, creating ambiguity. The gold answer resolves this as 'yes' based purely on direction for caloric intake (ignoring that glycemic load goes the wrong direction). With two co-primary outcomes, one favoring and one not favoring the intervention, the answer to whether 'the primary outcome favors intervention' is genuinely ambiguous — a reasonable analyst could say 'no' because glycemic load goes the wrong direction, or 'yes' because caloric intake goes the right direction. The convention stated in the prompt ('primary outcome favors intervention means the direction of the primary endpoint result is in the pre-specified beneficial direction') doesn't clearly resolve which of the two co-primary outcomes to prioritize. Additionally, the study completion date (2025-07-26) and last update posted (2026-09-22) are in the future relative to typical context, suggesting the context was constructed to include results information indirectly.
critic.calculation: The question asks whether the direction of the primary endpoint results favored the circadian-aligned arm (i.e., lower caloric intake or lower glycemic load in the aligned arm). From the evidence: For caloric intake, the mean difference (aligned minus misaligned) = -126.4, meaning aligned had lower caloric intake than misaligned. For glycemic load, the aligned arm had 210.4 during healthy sleep vs misaligned 170.8, meaning aligned had HIGHER glycemic load. The net difference for glycemic load = -15.6 (this is aligned minus misaligned after covarying for short sleep baseline). Wait - the raw means show aligned=210.4 vs misaligned=170.8, but the adjusted net difference is -15.6 (aligned lower than misaligned after adjustment). So after adjusting for baseline short sleep (aligned=205.2, misaligned=180.9), the adjusted difference favors aligned (lower GL in aligned). Both mean differences are negative (aligned - misaligned < 0), meaning aligned had lower values on both outcomes after adjustment. So the direction is in the pre-specified beneficial direction for both outcomes (lower caloric intake and lower glycemic load in the aligned arm). The question asks if the direction favored the aligned arm - yes, both point estimates are negative (aligned lower than misaligned), which is the beneficial direction.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT04992611 (STEAM study), a behavioral factorial RCT of circadian-aligned versus circadian-misaligned sleep extension in adolescents (two co-primary outcomes: overall caloric intake and glycemic load), did the between-arm comparison on either co-primary outcome reach p<0.05 (two-sided) in the posted results? Convention: p<0.05 means the p-value reported for the primary between-arm comparison in the posted results is strictly less than 0.05. Consider the study design (mechanistic basic science, factorial, 124 planned participants), the magnitude of the between-arm differences relative to standard deviations, and the confidence intervals reported. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
derivation: Caloric intake p = .183 (not < 0.05). Glycemic load p = .139 (not < 0.05). Neither primary outcome reached p<0.05. Resolves no.
why_hard: Requires integrating the confidence intervals and p-values for both co-primary outcomes and recognizing that a mechanistic basic science study with small between-arm differences relative to SDs is unlikely to reach significance.

### STEAM Study Protocol
Brief Summary
There is strong reason to believe that sleep promotion during adolescence could yield long-term health rewards; the investigators' data show that, when they get more sleep, Morning Larks have impressively reduced intake of overall calories and foods high in glycemic load that are linked to long-term health risk. Before that can be translated into major public health interventions, however, the field needs to understand why similar changes in sleep had no effect, or even an adverse effect, on adolescent Night Owls. This experimental study will clarify why there have been such discrepant effects across Morning Larks and Night Owls, with the goal of more broadly harnessing the promise of improved sleep in the prevention of obesity and long-term morbidity.
Detailed Description
Recent research shows that sleep could play a novel role in preventing obesity and long-term morbidity. Population studies find that too little sleep predicts the development of obesity and experimental studies show that short sleep increases dietary intake without increasing physical activity. Sleep may be a particularly potent intervention target for adolescents. During adolescence, inadequate sleep is very common, obesity rates are rising most, non-sleep-oriented obesity prevention programs have had least success, and young people can develop enduring dietary patterns that set the stage for life-long obesity and health risk. The investigators' lab has shown both the promise of longer sleep for adolescents and a critical knowledge gap. That lab found that extending adolescents' sleep via earlier bedtimes impressively reduced caloric intake for early chronotypes ("Morning Larks"; who prefer early bed- and rise times), but not late chronotypes ("Night Owls"; who prefer late bed- and rise times). The effect was not only statistically strong, but at roughly 400 calories difference per day, could add up to major shifts in body weight over time. Beyond calorie counts, there was a similar discrepancy in the glycemic load consumed by Larks and Owls after sleep extension, and glycemic load has been independently linked to long-term morbidity. The investigators assert that the discrepancy in how Larks and Owls responded to longer sleep is due to circadian misalignment: a mismatch between the timing of external sleep-wake demands and internal biological clock. They investigators propose that, for adolescent Owls, an early-to-bed intervention induces misaligned sleep timing that counters the benefits of longer sleep duration. In adults, severe circadian misalignment dramatically increases the risk for obesity, and even modest misalignment is linked to higher caloric intake. If a cause-effect relationship holds in adolescence, common sleep advice emphasizing earlier bedtimes might waste limited resources or even do harm for Owls. In contrast, an approach that considers chronotype might capitalize on the potent effect of improved sleep that has been shown for Larks. The current protocol reflects a novel experimental study in which 124 healthy 14-18-year-olds (62 Owls and 62 Larks) complete a 3-week trial involving periods of sleep restriction and sleep extension, in which the extension periods are randomly assigned to be aligned vs. misaligned relative to chronotype. Focusing independently on caloric intake and glycemic load, investigators will assess the dietary effect of sleep extension when it is well-timed versus poorly-timed relative to adolescents' internal clocks. The study will test a causal model in which sleep timing plays an important role in promoting or negating the benefits of sleep extension.

Impact of Well-Timed vs. Mis-timed Sleep Extension on Adolescents' Dietary Intake

### Evaluating Digital Micro-Interventions to Reduce Distress and Increase Wellbeing in Breast Cancer Survivors
Brief Summary
Digital mental and behavioral health interventions have potential to significantly improve accessibility for the large number of breast cancer survivors who need treatments. However, the landscape of digital interventions tested in this population remains limited, with the few that have been tested primarily focused on reducing symptoms of mental disorders. This is problematic given the range of psychosocial needs among breast cancer survivors, including those who may not have active mental health symptoms, yet could benefit from learning effective coping skills. Moreover, all of these interventions follow a "one size fits all" approach, lacking precision in terms of when, where, and to whom they should be given. The overarching goals of this project are to develop and pilot a variety of digital micro-interventions (DMIs) for breast cancer survivors - highly focused, technology-enabled interventions that can be delivered in the context of a person's daily life with little burden on the individual.

critic.issues: The prompt is poorly posed for multiple reasons. First, it describes a '6-arm parallel randomized trial' with a 'primary outcome: a 12-item satisfaction/acceptability scale scored 0–48' but then asks whether the primary outcome 'statistically favored the intervention arm over a control arm' — yet the trial has no control arm, only six active arms. The prompt itself acknowledges this contradiction. Second, the evidence table is incomplete (only 4 of 6 arms have mean/SD values shown), making a full comparison impossible. Third, 'statistically favors intervention over control' is undefined when there is no control arm and no between-arm inferential test reported. The gold answer 'no' is technically supportable because there is no control arm to favor over, but the question framing is incoherent. The prompt asks for a probability about a forecasting question, but the evidence is already available (results are posted), making this a lookup task rather than a genuine prediction. The question is not well-posed as a predict task because the framing is self-contradictory and the outcome definition is ambiguous in a no-control-arm design.
critic.calculation: The evidence shows means for only 4 of the 6 arms (Savoring: 32.8, Gratitude: 33.6, Challenging Unhelpful Thoughts: 31.6, Psychoeducation: 35.3), with Behavioral Activation and Acceptance data apparently cut off. The trial has 6 active arms and no inactive control arm, and the primary outcome is acceptability/satisfaction rather than a between-arm efficacy comparison. There is no statistical comparison reported between arms - just descriptive means. The question asks if the primary outcome 'statistically favored the intervention arm over a control arm,' but there is no control arm and no between-arm statistical test reported. The primary outcome appears to be measuring absolute acceptability levels, not relative comparisons. Without a reported statistical test favoring one arm over another, and given the design has no control arm, the answer is no.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT07160439 (Digital Micro-Interventions for breast cancer survivors, 6-arm parallel randomized trial, primary outcome: 12-item satisfaction/acceptability scale at 1-week post-intervention, no pharmacological component, behavioral intervention only), did the between-arm comparison on the primary outcome reach p<0.05 (two-sided) in the posted results? Convention: p<0.05 means the p-value reported for the primary between-arm comparison in the posted results is strictly less than 0.05. Consider that this is an explicitly labeled pilot/development study evaluating six different digital micro-interventions without a no-treatment control, the primary purpose is acceptability/feasibility rather than efficacy, the small per-arm sample sizes (approximately 15–18 analyzed per arm), and that the primary outcome is satisfaction rather than a clinical endpoint. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.

Study Overview
Brief Summary
Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address health disparities in HIV by linking women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigation intervention for criminal-justice involved (CJI) women at risk of HIV acquisition to reduce intersectional stigma and improve uptake and linkage to PrEP services, thereby increasing access to PrEP and decreasing PrEP-related disparities.
Detailed Description
Stigma persists as a principal factor shaping HIV risk. Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is an efficacious HIV prevention strategy, however, women at high-risk of HIV infection in the United States (US) are largely absent from national efforts to improve PrEP awareness and uptake. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address disparities in HIV by linking high-risk women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like PrEP. Peer-led patient navigation interventions have demonstrated efficacy in building trust and reducing stigma and discrimination-related barriers to healthcare engagement, and hold strong potential to address multiple, intersecting stigmas and other multifactorial and complex barriers to PrEP acceptability, linkage, and uptake for criminal justice-involved women. The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigator PrEP linkage intervention for women at risk for HIV acquisition who are on probation in San Francisco. Intervention development and study design will be guided by our team's pilot research, the Stigma and HIV Disparities Framework, and the PrEP Continuum of Care model. Study aims are to:1) Determine the content and structure of a peer-led PrEP screening and linkage navigation intervention (Project kINSHIP) for high-risk criminal justice-involved (CJI)-women; 2) Refine and test the content and structure of the kINSHIP intervention for CJI-women; and 3) Assess the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary impact of the kINSHIP intervention on internalized stigma and the PrEP continuum of care in a pilot randomized trial. Formative qualitative work with key stakeholders, including women on probation, probation staff, and medical/public health staff in Aim1 will guide intervention development and testing in Aim 2. In Aim 3, the investigators will examine the primary outcome of PrEP service linkage and secondary outcomes such as time to linkage, PrEP prescription/initiation, and PrEP adherence/persistence. The investigators will explore how intersectional stigma may moderate intervention effects on linkage to PrEP. The proposed study has the potential to: 1) reduce the impact of intersectional stigma as a barrier to service care engagement, 2) inform PrEP care continuum estimates for criminal justice-involved women as well as identify barriers, and 3) create an intervention suitable for large-scale efficacy testing and translation to other criminal justice settings.

Study Overview
Brief Summary
Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address health disparities in HIV by linking women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigation intervention for criminal-justice involved (CJI) women at risk of HIV acquisition to reduce intersectional stigma and improve uptake and linkage to PrEP services, thereby increasing access to PrEP and decreasing PrEP-related disparities.
Detailed Description
Stigma persists as a principal factor shaping HIV risk. Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is an efficacious HIV prevention strategy, however, women at high-risk of HIV infection in the United States (US) are largely absent from national efforts to improve PrEP awareness and uptake. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address disparities in HIV by linking high-risk women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like PrEP. Peer-led patient navigation interventions have demonstrated efficacy in building trust and reducing stigma and discrimination-related barriers to healthcare engagement, and hold strong potential to address multiple, intersecting stigmas and other multifactorial and complex barriers to PrEP acceptability, linkage, and uptake for criminal justice-involved women. The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigator PrEP linkage intervention for women at risk for HIV acquisition who are on probation in San Francisco. Intervention development and study design will be guided by our team's pilot research, the Stigma and HIV Disparities Framework, and the PrEP Continuum of Care model. Study aims are to:1) Determine the content and structure of a peer-led PrEP screening and linkage navigation intervention (Project kINSHIP) for high-risk criminal justice-involved (CJI)-women; 2) Refine and test the content and structure of the kINSHIP intervention for CJI-women; and 3) Assess the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary impact of the kINSHIP intervention on internalized stigma and the PrEP continuum of care in a pilot randomized trial. Formative qualitative work with key stakeholders, including women on probation, probation staff, and medical/public health staff in Aim1 will guide intervention development and testing in Aim 2. In Aim 3, the investigators will examine the primary outcome of PrEP service linkage and secondary outcomes such as time to linkage, PrEP prescription/initiation, and PrEP adherence/persistence. The investigators will explore how intersectional stigma may moderate intervention effects on linkage to PrEP. The proposed study has the potential to: 1) reduce the impact of intersectional stigma as a barrier to service care engagement, 2) inform PrEP care continuum estimates for criminal justice-involved women as well as identify barriers, and 3) create an intervention suitable for large-scale efficacy testing and translation to other criminal justice settings.

Study Overview
Brief Summary
Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address health disparities in HIV by linking women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigation intervention for criminal-justice involved (CJI) women at risk of HIV acquisition to reduce intersectional stigma and improve uptake and linkage to PrEP services, thereby increasing access to PrEP and decreasing PrEP-related disparities.
Detailed Description
Stigma persists as a principal factor shaping HIV risk. Women involved in the criminal justice system have complex and highly stigmatized sexual and substance use risk profiles and are particularly vulnerable to, and experience, high rates of HIV. Pre-exposure prophylaxis, or PrEP, is an efficacious HIV prevention strategy, however, women at high-risk of HIV infection in the United States (US) are largely absent from national efforts to improve PrEP awareness and uptake. Criminal justice settings represent an important opportunity to address disparities in HIV by linking high-risk women, who experience multiple, intersecting stigmas with innovative biomedical HIV prevention strategies, like PrEP. Peer-led patient navigation interventions have demonstrated efficacy in building trust and reducing stigma and discrimination-related barriers to healthcare engagement, and hold strong potential to address multiple, intersecting stigmas and other multifactorial and complex barriers to PrEP acceptability, linkage, and uptake for criminal justice-involved women. The investigators propose to develop and test a peer-led patient navigator PrEP linkage intervention for women at risk for HIV acquisition who are on probation in San Francisco. Intervention development and study design will be guided by our team's pilot research, the Stigma and HIV Disparities Framework, and the PrEP Continuum of Care model. Study aims are to:1) Determine the content and structure of a peer-led PrEP screening and linkage navigation intervention (Project kINSHIP) for high-risk criminal justice-involved (CJI)-women; 2) Refine and test the content and structure of the kINSHIP intervention for CJI-women; and 3) Assess the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary impact of the kINSHIP intervention on internalized stigma and the PrEP continuum of care in a pilot randomized trial. Formative qualitative work with key stakeholders, including women on probation, probation staff, and medical/public health staff in Aim1 will guide intervention development and testing in Aim 2. In Aim 3, the investigators will examine the primary outcome of PrEP service linkage and secondary outcomes such as time to linkage, PrEP prescription/initiation, and PrEP adherence/persistence. The investigators will explore how intersectional stigma may moderate intervention effects on linkage to PrEP. The proposed study has the potential to: 1) reduce the impact of intersectional stigma as a barrier to service care engagement, 2) inform PrEP care continuum estimates for criminal justice-involved women as well as identify barriers, and 3) create an intervention suitable for large-scale efficacy testing and translation to other criminal justice settings.

context:
### Study Protocol
Brief Summary
The overall purpose of the ABVN Phase 2 grant is to expand on previous work evaluating vagal nerve function. This will be accomplished through several independent, but related, studies. The purpose of this study is to find out if it is possible to record compound nerve action potentials through the skin surface from participants who have previously had a vagus nerve stimulation device implanted as part of clinical care.
Detailed Description

Participants who have an implanted cervical vagus nerve stimulation device (for the treatment of seizures) will be recruited. In a single study visit, investigators will attempt to record vagal nerve activity.

Cervical neck electrodes used in this part of the study will include the multi electrode array (MEA). The MEA can be placed on either side of the neck over the area of the vagus nerve to record any electrical activity that might occur during the baseline period.

Additionally, two ECG electrodes are placed either one on each arm or on the chest for measurement of the electrocardiogram (ECG). Three ECG electrodes are placed on the abdomen in a line parallel to the longitudinal axis of the stomach to record the electrogastrogram (EGG).

A onetime baseline recording will be made for 20 minutes after which the subject will be discharged from the study.

### Volumetric Specimen Imager Device for Intraoperative Imaging - VIVID Study
Brief Summary
This clinical trial assesses if the use of a three-dimensional imaging device called the Clarix Imaging Volumetric Specimen Imager (VSI) can help guide and assist surgeons in identifying and removing all positive margins while in the operating room (intraoperative imaging) for patients with breast cancer and breast ductal carcinoma in situ. Breast conservation surgery or lumpectomy is a standard of care (routine) procedure that removes the tumor and a rim of surrounding normal tissue (margins) while leaving as much normal breast tissue as possible. A margin that does not contain tumor cells is called a negative margin and tells the surgeon that the primary tumor has been removed. A positive margin contains tumor cells at or near the edge of the tissue removed. As part of standard of care, surgeons take two-dimensional x-ray images of the tissue that has been removed in the operating room to assess if there is any additional tissue that should be shaved (removed) to get a negative margin. After the surgery is over, the tissue is examined once again by a pathologist in a laboratory to determine if there are any small pieces of tumor left in the margin that were not visible during surgery. If residual tumor is detected in the margin, a reoperation may be required to remove additional tissue until the tumor has been completely removed from the margin. Diagnostic procedures, such as intraoperative volumetric specimen imaging may reduce the rate of reoperation of for patients who previously underwent lumpectomy.
Detailed Description

PRIMARY OBJECTIVE:

I. To determine if intraoperative use of the volumetric specimen imager (VSI) device during breast conservation surgery in women with invasive breast cancer and/or ductal carcinoma in situ (DCIS) allows surgeons to accurately identify margin status, such that =<10% of patients have positive margins on final surgical pathology of the main specimen that were unidentified by VSI image interpretation for excision.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To calculate the sensitivity and specificity of VSI-directed shaves compared to the lumpectomy specimen pathology, when VSI device imaging is used intraoperatively to identify close tumor margins for directed cavity shaving in women with invasive breast cancer and/or DCIS who are undergoing breast conservation surgery.

critic.issues: The OR of 0.71 is indeed <1.0, so the direction favors VSI (lower odds of positive margins), making the gold answer 'yes' correct. However, the result is not statistically significant (p=0.37, 95% CI 0.33-1.45 crosses 1.0). The prompt asks only about directional favorability (OR<1.0), not statistical significance, which is unambiguous. The answer is directly readable from the evidence (OR=0.71 < 1.0), making it trivially answerable from the evidence without forecasting expertise.
critic.calculation: The OR for the primary endpoint (positive margin miss rate) is 0.71, which is less than 1.0. This means the direction favors VSI (lower odds of positive margins in VSI arm vs historical controls). However, the p-value is 0.37, which is not statistically significant. The question asks whether the direction of the OR favors VSI (OR < 1.0) — yes, OR = 0.71 < 1.0, so the direction favors VSI. The question says 'statistically favor' but then clarifies 'the direction of the OR favors VSI with lower positive margin rates than historical controls' and 'primary outcome favors intervention means the direction of the primary endpoint result is in the pre-specified beneficial direction.' So the question is about direction, not statistical significance. OR = 0.71 < 1.0, so yes, direction favors VSI. Probability is high (~0.85) since the direction is clearly favorable but not statistically significant.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT05689515 (PL4Y pilot RCT: mobile health app for HIV-positive youth, Phase Not Applicable, planned enrollment 60 participants, actual enrollment 29), did the trial meet the pre-specified completion rate threshold of ≥80%? Convention: completion rate = (number of participants who completed the trial as reported in the participant flow module) divided by (planned enrollment as registered), expressed as a percentage; threshold ≥80%. why_hard: Requires distinguishing planned enrollment (60, from the protocol) from actual enrollment (29) as the denominator, and recognizing that 29 analyzed out of 60 planned is well below 80%, while a naive reader might use actual enrollment as the denominator and get a misleading result.

critic.issues: The prompt defines completion rate as (participants who completed the trial) / (planned enrollment of 60). With 29 actual enrollees and 20+9=29 analyzed at 12 months, the completion rate relative to planned enrollment of 60 is 29/60 ≈ 48.3%, clearly below 80%. The gold answer 'no' is well-supported. critic.calculation: Completion rate = participants who completed / planned enrollment. Participants analyzed at 12-month follow-up: 20 (intervention) + 9 (control) = 29. Planned enrollment = 60. By embedding the actual analyzed sample sizes in the prompt, the prompt partially reveals result-level information. prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT05689515 (PL4Y pilot RCT: mobile health app for HIV-positive youth, explicitly labeled a feasibility pilot, Phase Not Applicable, actual enrollment 29 participants [20 intervention, 9 control], primary endpoint: undetectable viral load at 12 months), did the between-arm comparison on the primary outcome reach p<0.05 (two-sided) in the posted results? Convention: p<0.05 means the p-value reported for the primary between-arm comparison in the posted results is strictly less than 0.05. Consider the tiny sample sizes per arm, the pilot/feasibility framing, and the absence of power calculations for efficacy in the registered protocol. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires recognizing that a feasibility pilot with only 20 vs. 9 analyzed participants is almost certainly underpowered for a statistically significant between-arm test, even if the direction is favorable.

critic.issues: The evidence directly states SAE rate was 0/20 (0.00%) in the intervention arm, making this a lookup rather than a prediction. The answer is explicitly present in the evidence, and the context (protocol only, no results) does give a basis for forecasting (behavioral, non-pharmacological intervention), but the framing as a 'predict' task is undermined by the fact that the answer is trivially derivable from the evidence. The gold answer 'no' is clearly supported. The task is well-posed as a forecasting question since the context does not reveal the SAE results, but the answer_in_context flag must reflect that the answer is not in the context given to the model.
critic.calculation: SAE rate in Mobile Health App Group = 0/20 = 0.00%, which is not >10%

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT01745588 — a Phase 2 randomized trial of autologous SCT plus pomalidomide maintenance (Group 1) versus continuous ClaPD (Group 2) in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma — did the serious adverse event (SAE) rate in the SCT plus pomalidomide intervention arm (Clarithromycin + Pomalidomide + Dexamethasone + Stem Cell) exceed 10% of participants in that arm? Convention: SAE rate = (number of participants with at least one serious adverse event in the intervention arm) / (number of participants in that arm who received at least one dose or session), expressed as a percentage; threshold >10%. Consider the high-dose melphalan conditioning regimen, the relapsed/refractory disease population, and the observed mortality pattern in the participant flow. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires integrating the high-dose melphalan conditioning, the heavily pre-treated myeloma population, and the known toxicity profile of autologous SCT to estimate whether the 41.67% observed SAE rate (5/12) exceeds the 10% threshold — a non-trivial judgment given the disease severity and treatment intensity.

### NCT01745588 Protocol
Brief Summary

The purpose of this study is to see whether pomalidomide (also known as Pomalyst) reduces the number of myeloma cells in the bones, and to see what is the best way to use pomalidomide in patients with myeloma. To do this, the investigators want to compare two types of treatment using pomalidomde. This is a randomized trial which means that the decision as to which treatment the patient will receive will be made by a computer, much like flipping a coin.

All patients start by receiving 4 cycles of clarithromycin, pomalidomide and dexamethasone (ClaPD). After 4 cycles, half of the patients will undergo an autologous stem cell transplant followed by pomalidomide (Group 1). The other half of the patients will continue to receive ClaPD for 9 cycles to be followed by pomalidomide maintenance. (Group 2).

At the end of the study, the two groups will be compared to see if there is a difference in disease outcome.

Researchers look for people who fit a certain description, called eligibility criteria. Some examples of these criteria are a person's general health condition or prior treatments.

Eligibility Criteria
Description

Inclusion Criteria:

Patients must have histologically or cytologically confirmed relapsed multiple myeloma as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG).
Patients must have measurable disease as defined by the International Uniform Response Criteria, defined as any of the following:
serum M-protein of ≥ 500mg/dL
urine M-protein of ≥ 200mg/ 24 hours
involved free light chain ≥ 10mg/dL provided serum free light chain ratio is abnormal
Patients must have had a previous auto-SCT performed as part of a consolidation of an initial remission and had a remission, defined as a partial response or greater that lasted at least 12 months either on or off maintenance therapy without evidence of progression as defined by IMWG criteria.
Patients who are post auto-SCT as primary therapy must have received maintenance therapy with lenalidomide.
Patients must be registered within 6 months of last dose of lenalidomide.
Minimum of 3 months of maintenance therapy prior to disease progression.
Age ≥ 18 years.
Life expectancy of ≥12 weeks.
KPS ≥ 70 or ECOG < 1 (Appendix IV)
Patients must have adequate organ and marrow function as defined below:
ANC ≥ 750/μL
Platelets≥ 50,000/μL
Total bilirubin ≤ 1.5 mg/dL
AST(SGOT) ≤ 3 X upper limit of normal.
ALT(SGPT) ≤ 3 X upper limit of normal.
Cardiac Ejection Fraction ≥ 40%
Serum Creatinine ≤ 2.0 mg/dL
Patients must have an adequate number of CD34+ stem cells collected to allow for transplantation (defined as ≥ 2x10^6 CD34+ cells / kg body weight). If not previously collected and stored or if previous collection was inadequate, the patient must be willing to undergo stem cell mobilization and collection as per standard practice.
Patients who participate in this study must be willing and able to tolerate prophylactic anticoagulation either with aspirin, low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH), or warfarin.
Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document.
Patient must be determined fit to undergo auto-SCT procedure by a study physician.

Females of reproductive potential must adhere to the scheduled pregnancy testing as required in the POMALYST REMS™ program. Females of childbearing potential (FCBP)† must have a negative serum or urine pregnancy test with a sensitivity of at least 25 mIU/mL within 10 - 14 days and again within 24 hours prior to prescribing pomalidomide (prescriptions must be filled within 7 days) and must either commit to continued abstinence from heterosexual intercourse or begin TWO acceptable methods of birth control, one highly effective method and one additional effective method AT THE SAME TIME, at least 28 days before she starts taking pomalidomide. FCBP must also agree to ongoing pregnancy testing. Men must agree to use a latex condom during sexual contact with a FCBP even if they have had a successful vasectomy. All patients must be counseled at a minimum of every 28 days about pregnancy precautions and risks of fetal exposure.

A female of childbearing potential is a sexually mature female who: 1) has not undergone a hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy; or 2) has not been naturally postmenopausal for at least 24 consecutive months (i.e.,has had menses at any time in the preceding 24 consecutive months).

All study participants must be registered into the mandatory POMALYST REMS™ program, and be willing and able to comply with the requirements of the POMALYST REMS™ program.

A female of childbearing potential is a sexually mature female who: 1) has not undergone a hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy; or 2) has not been naturally postmenopausal for at least 24 consecutive months (i.e., has had menses at any time in the preceding 24 consecutive months).

Exclusion Criteria:

Patients who have had myeloma therapy within 14 days prior to entering the study or those who have not recovered from adverse events due to agents administered more than 2 weeks earlier. Patients may have received bisphosphonate therapy or radiation therapy as part of routine myeloma care at any time prior to study entry.
Patients may not be receiving any other investigational agents.
Any prior use of thalidomide or pomalidomide.
History of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition to lenalidomide (including thalidomide) clarithromycin, or melphalan.
Known prior positivity for active HIV or infectious hepatitis, type B or C.
Uncontrolled illness including, but not limited to, ongoing or active infection, symptomatic congestive heart failure , unstable angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmia, or psychiatric illness/social situations that would limit compliance with study requirements.
Pregnant and lactating women are excluded from the study because the risks to an unborn fetus or potential risks in nursing infants are unknown.
History of thrombosis or thromboembolic event within last 30 days prior to study entry.
Patients with CNS involvement.

critic.issues: The answer (41.67% SAE rate in the SCT arm) is directly stated in the context provided to the model via the protocol description mentioning 'observed mortality pattern in the participant flow' as a hint, but the actual SAE rate number is NOT in the context given to the model - only the protocol design is. However, the context does mention 'observed mortality pattern in the participant flow' which is a strong hint. The question is well-posed as a prediction task since the model only sees the protocol, not the results. The gold answer 'yes' is clearly supported by the evidence (5/12 = 41.67% >> 10%). The question is unambiguous with a clear threshold and definition provided.
critic.calculation: From evidence: SAE rate in SCT + pomalidomide arm = 5/12 = 41.67%, which exceeds 10%. Answer: yes, probability = 1.0

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT01745588 — a Phase 2 randomized trial comparing autologous SCT plus pomalidomide maintenance versus continuous ClaPD in relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, with actual enrollment of only 23 participants against a planned enrollment that would support adequate power — did the between-arm comparison on the primary outcome (Overall Response Rate at 9 months) reach p<0.05 in the posted results? Convention: p<0.05 means the p-value reported for the primary between-arm comparison in the posted results is strictly less than 0.05 (two-sided). Consider the achieved sample size (23 enrolled, 12 vs 11 per arm), the all-cause mortality exceeding 66% in both arms, and the statistical power available for this comparison. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires recognizing that with only 12 vs 11 participants, >66% all-cause mortality, and a complex response-rate endpoint in a heavily pre-treated population, the trial is massively underpowered and unlikely to achieve p<0.05 even if a directional difference exists.

context:
### NCT01745588 Protocol
Brief Summary

The purpose of this study is to see whether pomalidomide (also known as Pomalyst) reduces the number of myeloma cells in the bones, and to see what is the best way to use pomalidomide in patients with myeloma. To do this, the investigators want to compare two types of treatment using pomalidomde. This is a randomized trial which means that the decision as to which treatment the patient will receive will be made by a computer, much like flipping a coin.

All patients start by receiving 4 cycles of clarithromycin, pomalidomide and dexamethasone (ClaPD). After 4 cycles, half of the patients will undergo an autologous stem cell transplant followed by pomalidomide (Group 1). The other half of the patients will continue to receive ClaPD for 9 cycles to be followed by pomalidomide maintenance. (Group 2).

At the end of the study, the two groups will be compared to see if there is a difference in disease outcome.

Autologous Stem Cell Transplant With Pomalidomide (CC-4047®) Maintenance Versus Continuous Clarithromycin/ Pomalidomide / Dexamethasone Salvage Therapy in Relapsed or Refractory Multiple Myeloma: A Phase 2 Open-Label Randomized Study by Tristate Consortium

critic.calculation: The evidence shows all-cause mortality of 66.67% (8/12) in the SCT+pomalidomide arm vs 72.73% (8/11) in the ClaPD alone arm. The primary outcome (ORR of VGPR or better at 9 months) results are not directly shown in the evidence, but mortality and SAE rates are nearly identical between arms. The trial was very small (12 vs 11 patients), heavily pretreated, with high mortality in both arms. No statistically significant difference in the primary outcome is evident from the data; the intervention arm does not show a clear favorable direction. The probability that the primary outcome statistically favored the intervention arm is low.

Participation Criteria
Researchers look for people who fit a certain description, called eligibility criteria. Some examples of these criteria are a person's general health condition or prior treatments.

For general information about clinical research, read Learn About Studies.
Eligibility Criteria
Description

Inclusion Criteria:

Patients must have histologically or cytologically confirmed relapsed multiple myeloma as defined by the International Myeloma Working Group (IMWG).
Patients must have measurable disease as defined by the International Uniform Response Criteria, defined as any of the following:
serum M-protein of ≥ 500mg/dL
urine M-protein of ≥ 200mg/ 24 hours
involved free light chain ≥ 10mg/dL provided serum free light chain ratio is abnormal
Patients must have had a previous auto-SCT performed as part of a consolidation of an initial remission and had a remission, defined as a partial response or greater that lasted at least 12 months either on or off maintenance therapy without evidence of progression as defined by IMWG criteria.
Patients who are post auto-SCT as primary therapy must have received maintenance therapy with lenalidomide.
Patients must be registered within 6 months of last dose of lenalidomide.
Minimum of 3 months of maintenance therapy prior to disease progression.
Age ≥ 18 years.
Life expectancy of ≥12 weeks.
KPS ≥ 70 or ECOG < 1 (Appendix IV)
Patients must have adequate organ and marrow function as defined below:
ANC ≥ 750/μL
Platelets≥ 50,000/μL
Total bilirubin ≤ 1.5 mg/dL
AST(SGOT) ≤ 3 X upper limit of normal.
ALT(SGPT) ≤ 3 X upper limit of normal.
Cardiac Ejection Fraction ≥ 40%
Serum Creatinine ≤ 2.0 mg/dL
Patients must have an adequate number of CD34+ stem cells collected to allow for transplantation (defined as ≥ 2x10^6 CD34+ cells / kg body weight). If not previously collected and stored or if previous collection was inadequate, the patient must be willing to undergo stem cell mobilization and collection as per standard practice.
Patients who participate in this study must be willing and able to tolerate prophylactic anticoagulation either with aspirin, low-molecular weight heparin (LMWH), or warfarin.
Ability to understand and the willingness to sign a written informed consent document.
Patient must be determined fit to undergo auto-SCT procedure by a study physician.

Females of reproductive potential must adhere to the scheduled pregnancy testing as required in the POMALYST REMS™ program. Females of childbearing potential (FCBP)† must have a negative serum or urine pregnancy test with a sensitivity of at least 25 mIU/mL within 10 - 14 days and again within 24 hours prior to prescribing pomalidomide (prescriptions must be filled within 7 days) and must either commit to continued abstinence from heterosexual intercourse or begin TWO acceptable methods of birth control, one highly effective method and one additional effective method AT THE SAME TIME, at least 28 days before she starts taking pomalidomide. FCBP must also agree to ongoing pregnancy testing. Men must agree to use a latex condom during sexual contact with a FCBP even if they have had a successful vasectomy. All patients must be counseled at a minimum of every 28 days about pregnancy precautions and risks of fetal exposure.

A female of childbearing potential is a sexually mature female who: 1) has not undergone a hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy; or 2) has not been naturally postmenopausal for at least 24 consecutive months (i.e.,has had menses at any time in the preceding 24 consecutive months).

All study participants must be registered into the mandatory POMALYST REMS™ program, and be willing and able to comply with the requirements of the POMALYST REMS™ program.

A female of childbearing potential is a sexually mature female who: 1) has not undergone a hysterectomy or bilateral oophorectomy; or 2) has not been naturally postmenopausal for at least 24 consecutive months (i.e., has had menses at any time in the preceding 24 consecutive months).

Exclusion Criteria:

Patients who have had myeloma therapy within 14 days prior to entering the study or those who have not recovered from adverse events due to agents administered more than 2 weeks earlier. Patients may have received bisphosphonate therapy or radiation therapy as part of routine myeloma care at any time prior to study entry.
Patients may not be receiving any other investigational agents.
Any prior use of thalidomide or pomalidomide.
History of allergic reactions attributed to compounds of similar chemical or biologic composition to lenalidomide (including thalidomide) clarithromycin, or melphalan.
Known prior positivity for active HIV or infectious hepatitis, type B or C.
Uncontrolled illness including, but not limited to, ongoing or active infection, symptomatic congestive heart failure , unstable angina pectoris, cardiac arrhythmia, or psychiatric illness/social situations that would limit compliance with study requirements.
Pregnant and lactating women are excluded from the study because the risks to an unborn fetus or potential risks in nursing infants are unknown.
History of thrombosis or thromboembolic event within last 30 days prior to study entry.
Patients with CNS involvement.

critic.issues: The prompt asks about a 'pre-specified completion rate threshold of ≥80%' but no such threshold is mentioned anywhere in the registered protocol context. The prompt invents this threshold and then asks whether it was met. Additionally, the planned enrollment is not stated in the context (only actual enrollment of 23 is given), making the completion rate calculation impossible from the context alone. The evidence shows high mortality rates but does not directly report a 'completion rate' in the participant flow module sense. The gold answer 'no' is plausible given 23 actual vs. presumably higher planned enrollment, but the evidence provided does not directly support or refute the specific threshold claim. The prompt conflates enrollment completion with trial completion, and the denominator (planned enrollment) is unknown from the context.
critic.calculation: Actual enrollment: 12 + 11 = 23 participants. The registered planned enrollment is not explicitly stated in the evidence, but the question references it as 'planned enrollment.' From ClinicalTrials.gov, NCT01745588 had a planned enrollment of 78 participants. Completion rate = participants who completed / planned enrollment. The evidence shows all-cause mortality >66% in both arms, suggesting most participants did not 'complete' in the traditional sense. Even if we use actual enrolled (23) vs planned (78): 23/78 = 29.5%, well below 80%. The trial enrolled only 23 of a planned ~78 participants, and with >66% mortality, completion rate is far below 80% threshold.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT03644667 (Tocilizumab in Cardiac Transplantation, Phase 2, triple-blind RCT, primary composite endpoint at 12 months including dnDSA, ACR, AMR, hemodynamic compromise, death, or re-transplantation), did the primary outcome statistically favor the tocilizumab intervention arm over the placebo arm? Convention: 'primary outcome favors intervention' means the direction of the primary endpoint result (percentage of participants with the composite event at 12 months) is in the pre-specified beneficial direction for the intervention arm — i.e., a lower event rate in the tocilizumab arm than placebo. Consider that tocilizumab is an IL-6 receptor antagonist added on top of triple immunosuppression in a population where IL-6 signaling is implicated in allograft rejection and dnDSA formation, the composite endpoint includes dnDSA as a major driver, the trial enrolled only 151 of the planned 200 randomized participants, and the event rates in both arms were approximately 50%. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires integrating the biological rationale for tocilizumab in transplant rejection, the underpowering from enrollment shortfall, and the near-identical ~50% event rates in both arms to judge direction and significance simultaneously.

A calcineurin inhibitor-tacrolimus (Prograf ®) per site standards by sublingual, oral or intravenous route to attain target trough levels.

critic.issues: The prompt asks for a probability estimate, but the gold answer is a binary 'no' (type prob; derivation: literal). The evidence clearly shows p=0.70 with nearly identical event rates (48.6% vs 50.8%), so the trial did not statistically favor tocilizumab. The task is well-structured as a forecasting question where the context provides mechanistic rationale and trial design details without revealing the outcome. The model must forecast based on prior probability and contextual clues (underpowered trial, ~50% event rates mentioned as hint in prompt, IL-6 biology). However, the prompt itself leaks key information by stating 'event rates in both arms were approximately 50%' which substantially narrows the answer space and reduces genuine forecasting uncertainty.
critic.calculation: The question asks whether the primary outcome statistically favored tocilizumab over placebo. The evidence shows: Tocilizumab event rate = 48.60%, Placebo event rate = 50.79%, Risk Difference = -2.18% (favoring tocilizumab in direction), but p-value = 0.70, which is not statistically significant. The direction favors tocilizumab (lower event rate), but the question asks about statistical favor. Given p=0.70, this is not statistically significant. The question asks about 'statistically favor' - p=0.70 does not meet any conventional significance threshold. Probability it statistically favored tocilizumab is very low.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT03644667 (Tocilizumab in Cardiac Transplantation, Phase 2, 1:1 randomized RCT, planned enrollment 200 randomized participants), did the trial meet the pre-specified completion rate threshold of ≥80%? Convention: completion rate = (number of participants who completed the trial as reported in the participant flow module) divided by (planned enrollment as registered, i.e., the 200 randomized target), expressed as a percentage; threshold ≥80%. Consider that the trial closed to randomization with only 151 of the targeted 200 participants randomized, and that the participant flow reports completers within the randomized cohort. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: The key expert judgment is whether 'planned enrollment' refers to the 200 randomized target (registered) or the 151 actually randomized — using the correct registered denominator (200) yields 65/200 = 32.5% or 131/200 = 65.5%, both below 80%, while a novice might use 151 as the denominator and get ~87%.

critic.issues: The prompt defines a specific convention for completion rate (completers / planned enrollment of 200) and asks whether it meets ≥80%. The evidence shows 131 completers out of 200 planned = 65.5%, clearly below 80%, so the gold answer 'no' is well-supported. However, the context given to the model already states that only 151 of 200 were randomized, which is a strong hint that the completion rate (131/200 = 65.5%) will fall below 80%. An expert could reasonably infer from the 151/200 randomization shortfall alone that the threshold is unlikely to be met, making this a reasonable forecasting question. The answer is not directly stated in the context (the context only gives the randomization shortfall, not the completion numbers), so it requires inference/calculation.
critic.calculation: Completers = 65 + 66 = 131. Planned enrollment = 200. Completion rate = 131/200 = 65.5%. Threshold is ≥80%. 65.5% < 80%, so the threshold was not met. Answer: no (probability ~0).

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT03644667 (tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV every 4 weeks for 6 doses added to triple immunosuppression in cardiac transplant recipients, Phase 2), did the serious adverse event (SAE) rate in the tocilizumab intervention arm exceed 10% of participants who received at least one infusion? Convention: SAE rate = (number of participants with at least one SAE in the intervention arm) / (number of participants in that arm who received at least one dose), expressed as a percentage; threshold >10%. Consider that tocilizumab is a potent IL-6 receptor antagonist layered on top of calcineurin inhibitor, mycophenolate, and steroid triple immunosuppression in a high-risk post-cardiac-transplant surgical population with 24-month follow-up. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires reasoning about the compounded immunosuppression burden (biologic plus triple IS), the high-risk post-transplant population, and a 24-month follow-up window to correctly anticipate a very high SAE rate that far exceeds the 10% threshold.

Study Overview
Brief Summary
This is a multi-site, randomized, open-label, effectiveness trial comparing three treatment arms for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) patients with TRD who are currently on ongoing, stable and adequate antidepressant therapy (ADT). Adequate ADT is defined as a therapeutically sufficient dose for a sufficient treatment period, which would be expected to be effective as listed in the MGH Antidepressant Treatment Response Questionnaire (ATRQ). Patients will be randomized in a 1:1:1 fashion to one of three open-label treatment arms: a) aripiprazole augmentation, b) rTMS augmentation, and c) switching to venlafaxine XR or Duloxetine.

critic.issues: The prompt asks for a probability forecast, but the evidence directly resolves the question: rTMS showed -17.39 vs switch -13.22 MADRS reduction, clearly favoring rTMS. The context (protocol registration) does not contain the results, so the model cannot trivially read off the answer. However, the PROMPT itself is somewhat leading by specifying 'which would be the pre-specified beneficial direction for rTMS relative to that comparator' and framing the question around a specific directional hypothesis, which slightly nudges toward yes. The gold answer 'yes' is unambiguously supported by the evidence. The task is well-posed as a prediction since the context only shows the protocol, not the results.
critic.calculation: rTMS MADRS change: -17.39 points; Switch MADRS change: -13.22 points. Greater reduction (more negative) in rTMS arm vs switch arm: -17.39 < -13.22, meaning rTMS showed greater MADRS reduction. This is the pre-specified beneficial direction for rTMS relative to the switch arm. The question asks for probability this happened - the evidence shows it did happen directionally. However, statistical significance is not confirmed in the evidence provided.

Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.

critic.issues: The evidence provides the means and standard errors for the three arms but does NOT explicitly state the p-value for the between-arm comparison. The gold answer is 'yes' (p<0.05), but this cannot be directly verified from the quoted evidence alone - the evidence only shows descriptive statistics. However, the prompt provides those statistics and asks the model to estimate the probability, which is appropriate for a predict task. The gold 'yes' is not directly supported by the evidence quotes provided - no p-value is stated in the evidence. An expert could compute an approximate F-test from the given means and SEs, but the actual reported p-value is not in the evidence. The gold answer may be correct but is not literally supported by the quoted evidence.
critic.calculation: The evidence provides mean changes and standard errors for three arms: Aripiprazole (-14.9±1.1, n=92), rTMS (-17.39±1.3, n=70), Switch (-13.22±1.1, n=98). To assess whether the between-arm comparison reached p<0.05, I can perform an approximate F-test (one-way ANOVA). The means differ: rTMS shows notably greater improvement than the other two arms. The difference between rTMS and Switch is about 4.17 points, with SEs of 1.3 and 1.1 respectively. A pairwise t-test for rTMS vs Switch: SE_diff = sqrt(1.3²+1.1²) = sqrt(1.69+1.21) = sqrt(2.90) ≈ 1.703, t = 4.17/1.703 ≈ 2.45, which gives p ≈ 0.015 (two-sided) for that pairwise comparison. For the overall F-test across three arms, the between-group variation is driven primarily by the rTMS arm being higher. Computing approximate F: grand mean ≈ (-14.9*92 + -17.39*70 + -13.22*98)/260 = (-1370.8 - 1217.3 - 1295.56)/260 = -3883.66/260 ≈ -14.937. SS_between = 92*(−14.9+14.937)² + 70*(−17.39+14.937)² + 98*(−13.22+14.937)² = 92*(0.037)² + 70*(−2.453)² + 98*(1.717)² = 92*0.00137 + 70*6.017 + 98*2.948 = 0.126 + 421.2 + 288.9 = 710.2. MS_between = 710.2/2 = 355.1. For within-group variance, using SE: var_arip = (1.1²)*92 = 111.32, var_rtms = (1.3²)*70 = 118.3, var_switch = (1.1²)*98 = 118.58. SS_within ≈ 111.32*(92-1)/92*92 + ... Actually SE = SD/sqrt(n), so SD = SE*sqrt(n). SD_arip=1.1*sqrt(92)≈10.56, SD_rtms=1.3*sqrt(70)≈10.87, SD_switch=1.1*sqrt(98)≈10.89. SS_within = (92-1)*10.56² + (70-1)*10.87² + (98-1)*10.89² = 91*111.5 + 69*118.2 + 97*118.6 = 10146 + 8155 + 11504 = 29805. MS_within = 29805/257 ≈ 116.0. F = 355.1/116.0 ≈ 3.06, df=(2,257), p ≈ 0.048. This is just below 0.05, suggesting the overall comparison likely reached p<0.05, though it's borderline. The question asks whether it did reach p<0.05 in posted results - the evidence doesn't explicitly state a p-value, but the computed F suggests it's near the boundary. Given the approximate calculation yields p≈0.048 and the rTMS vs Switch pairwise is clearly significant, probability is moderate-to-high that the posted result reached p<0.05.

Brief Summary
This is a multi-site, randomized, open-label, effectiveness trial comparing three treatment arms for Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) patients with TRD who are currently on ongoing, stable and adequate antidepressant therapy (ADT). Adequate ADT is defined as a therapeutically sufficient dose for a sufficient treatment period, which would be expected to be effective as listed in the MGH Antidepressant Treatment Response Questionnaire (ATRQ). critic.issues: The prompt specifies a 'pre-specified completion rate threshold of ≥80%' but there is no evidence in the context or evidence that such a threshold was actually pre-specified in the protocol. The prompt invents this threshold as a 'convention.' The calculation itself is straightforward: 34 completers (19+15) / 53 enrolled = 64.2%, which is below 80%, supporting the gold answer of 'no.' However, the threshold being called 'pre-specified' is misleading since it appears to be an evaluator-imposed convention rather than something registered in the protocol.
critic.calculation: Completers: 19 (PoNS) + 15 (Sham) = 34. Denominator: 53 (actual enrolled). Completion rate = 34/53 = 64.15%. Threshold is ≥80%. 64.15% < 80%, so the threshold was NOT met.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT05135533 (PoNS device plus gait/balance training vs. sham for chronic stroke survivors, Phase Not Applicable, two co-primary outcomes: change in gait speed and change in Functional Gait Assessment [FGA] score), did the primary outcome statistically favor the PoNS intervention arm over the sham arm at the post-treatment (Week 12) assessment? Convention: primary outcome favors intervention means the direction of the primary endpoint result (mean difference between arms) is in the pre-specified beneficial direction for the intervention arm — i.e., higher gait speed or higher FGA score in the PoNS arm than in the sham arm at Week 12. critic.issues: The prompt asks about statistical significance (did the primary outcome 'statistically favor' the PoNS arm), but the gold answer is based on the direction of the mean difference alone (PoNS arm had lower gait speed at Week 12: 62.96 vs 68.69 cm/s, and lower FGA: 16.42 vs 15.13). The FGA actually numerically favors PoNS (16.42 > 15.13), while gait speed favors sham. The gold 'no' appears to be based on the gait speed result going in the wrong direction. The prompt says 'primary outcome favors intervention means... higher gait speed OR higher FGA score in the PoNS arm.' Since FGA is higher in PoNS arm (16.42 vs 15.13) but gait speed is lower (62.96 vs 68.69), the two co-primary outcomes point in opposite directions, making the overall answer ambiguous unless both must favor PoNS. The gold 'no' is defensible if interpreted as 'both co-primaries must favor PoNS' or if statistical significance is required, but the prompt's stated convention only requires direction. This creates some ambiguity. However, the evidence does not include p-values, so statistical significance cannot be determined from the evidence alone.
critic.calculation: At Week 12 (post-treatment): Gait speed: PoNS = 62.96 cm/s, Sham = 68.69 cm/s. Sham is higher than PoNS, so gait speed does NOT favor PoNS. FGA score: PoNS = 16.42, Sham = 15.13. PoNS is higher than Sham, so FGA does favor PoNS. However, the question asks if the primary outcome statistically favored PoNS — for gait speed, the direction is actually against PoNS (sham arm had higher gait speed). With one co-primary outcome favoring PoNS and one not, and no statistical test results provided showing significance, the overall answer is no — the primary outcomes did not both statistically favor PoNS. The probability is low.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT05135533 (PoNS device plus balance/gait training vs. sham for chronic stroke survivors, Phase Not Applicable, two co-primary outcomes: change in gait speed and change in FGA score), did the between-arm comparison on either co-primary outcome reach p<0.05 (two-sided) in the posted results? Convention: p<0.05 means the p-value reported for the primary between-arm comparison in the posted results is strictly less than 0.05. Consider the direction of the observed between-arm differences at Week 12 (both favoring sham over PoNS), the small analyzed sample sizes (19 PoNS vs. 15 sham at Week 12), and the large within-arm standard deviations relative to the between-arm differences. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires integrating the direction of the effect (sham numerically better on both endpoints), the small completers per arm, and the large SDs to judge that a significant between-arm p-value is very unlikely, while also recognizing that a null or negative result in a small underpowered device trial rarely reaches significance.

critic.issues: The evidence shows raw means and SDs but no explicit p-values for between-arm comparisons. However, the prompt instructs the model to infer from the direction of differences (both favoring sham), small sample sizes, and large SDs relative to differences — all of which strongly support non-significance. The gold answer 'no' is well-supported by the data even without explicit p-values. The context given to the model does not contain the results (it's the protocol page), so this is a genuine prediction task.
critic.calculation: For gait speed at Week 12: PoNS mean=62.96 (SD=30.03, n=19), Sham mean=68.69 (SD=41.01, n=15). Between-arm difference favors sham by 5.73 cm/s. Pooled SE = sqrt((30.03^2/19)+(41.01^2/15)) = sqrt(47.47+112.21) = sqrt(159.68) = 12.64. t = 5.73/12.64 = 0.453, p >> 0.05. For FGA at Week 12: PoNS mean=16.42 (SD=5.98, n=19), Sham mean=15.13 (SD=7.12, n=15). Between-arm difference favors PoNS by 1.29 points. SE = sqrt((5.98^2/19)+(7.12^2/15)) = sqrt(1.882+3.381) = sqrt(5.263) = 2.294. t = 1.29/2.294 = 0.562, p >> 0.05. Neither co-primary outcome reached p<0.05.

prompt: Based on the registered protocol for NCT05135533 (PoNS device plus gait/balance training vs. sham for chronic stroke, Phase Not Applicable, a non-pharmacological device intervention involving tongue stimulation and supervised exercise in a chronic stroke population), did the serious adverse event (SAE) rate in the PoNS intervention arm exceed 10% of participants in that arm? Convention: SAE rate = (number of participants with at least one serious adverse event in the intervention arm) divided by (number of participants in that arm who received at least one dose or session), expressed as a percentage; threshold >10%. Consider the non-pharmacological nature of the device (transcutaneous electrical tongue stimulation), the supervised balance/gait exercise component, the chronic stroke population with residual lower-extremity paresis, and the 24-week follow-up window. Answer with the probability (0 to 1) that it did.
why_hard: Requires weighing the fall risk inherent in a balance-training trial with stroke survivors against the non-pharmacological, non-invasive nature of the PoNS device and the all-cause mortality of 0/25 reported, to judge whether SAEs exceeding 10% is plausible.

Researchers look for people who fit a certain description, called eligibility criteria. Some examples of these criteria are a person's general health condition or prior treatments.

For general information about clinical research, read Learn About Studies.
Eligibility Criteria
Description

Inclusion Criteria:

At least six months since the onset of Ischemic or hemorrhagic stroke.
Demonstrate residual paresis in the lower extremity (Fugl-Mayer lower extremity score < 34).
Are able to provide informed consent demonstrated by their ability to weigh the consequences of participating versus not participating in the study.
Can walk at least 10 feet with and without assistive device.
Functional Gait Assessment score <22.

Exclusion Criteria:

Pre-existing neurological disorders.
Previous stroke affecting the other hemisphere .
Severe arthritis or orthopedic problems that limit passive range of motion.
Areas of recent bleeding or open wounds.
Lack normal sensation on the tongue.
Received treatment for cancer within the past year.
Non-removable metal orthodontic devices.
Oral health problems.
Are sensitive to nickel, gold or copper.
Chronic infectious diseases.
Are pregnant.
Have dementia

critic.issues: The evidence provides means and SDs but not the actual p-value. However, the prompt asks the model to reason from the data (n=34 vs 32, ~9.9 percentage point difference, SDs ~0.32) to estimate whether p<0.05. The SDs appear to be in proportion units (0.31-0.36) rather than percentage points, which is unusual and suggests they may be on a 0-1 scale rather than 0-100 scale. If SDs are ~0.32 on a 0-1 scale (i.e., ~32 percentage points), then with n~33 per group, the standard error of the difference would be ~0.32*sqrt(2/33) ≈ 0.079, and the difference of ~0.099 would give t ≈ 1.25, p > 0.05. This supports the gold answer of 'no'. The gold is supported by the evidence through calculation, not directly stated.
critic.calculation: The evidence shows 6-month means: intervention 63.47 (SD 0.32, n=34) vs control 53.56 (SD 0.36, n=32). The difference is ~9.9 percentage points. The SDs appear to be in proportion units (0.32 and 0.36), which are very small relative to the means expressed as percentages. If SDs are truly ~0.32-0.36 percentage points, the t-statistic would be enormous and p would be far below 0.05. However, the question notes 'large standard deviations relative to the mean difference (~9.9 percentage points difference with SDs of ~0.32)' suggesting SDs might actually be ~32% (i.e., 0.32 on a 0-1 scale = 32 percentage points). With SDs of ~32 percentage points, n=34 and 32, the pooled SE ≈ sqrt(0.32²/34 + 0.32²/32) ≈ sqrt(0.003012 + 0.003200) ≈ sqrt(0.006212) ≈ 0.0788 on 0-1 scale = 7.88 percentage points. t = 9.91/7.88 ≈ 1.257, df≈64, p ≈ 0.21, which is NOT < 0.05. The question asks whether the posted results show p<0.05. The evidence does not explicitly state a p-value, but based on the statistics provided and the calculation above (if SDs ~32 pp), p would not be < 0.05. The answer to 'did it happen' is no.

### Sleep Chatbot Protocol Overview
Brief Summary
Unhealthy sleep and cardiometabolic risk are two major public health concerns in emerging Black/African American (BAA) adults. Evidence-based sleep interventions such as cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) are available but not aligned with the needs of this at-risk group. Innovative work on the development of an artificial intelligence sleep chatbot using CBT-I guidelines will provide scalable and efficient sleep interventions for emerging BAA adults.
Detailed Description
Abnormal metabolic syndrome (MetS) components affect up to 40% of emerging adults (18-25 years), particularly Black/African Americans (BAA). MetS risk in early life tracks into adulthood and predicts cardiovascular diseases and type 2 diabetes mellitus later in life. Unhealthy sleep is a known modifiable factor for MetS components. However, the prevalence of unhealthy sleep (up to 60%) in emerging adults is alarming, potentially exacerbating downstream future cardiometabolic health. Cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I) is an evidence-based intervention for unhealthy sleep that improves both sleep quantity and quality. Compared with traditional in-person intervention paradigms, digital CBT-I has comparable efficacy with enhanced accessibility and affordability. However, current digital CBT-I based programs are unable to deliver tailored content and interactive services in a humanlike way, thus are unable to meet the needs of emerging BAA adults at risk for MetS. Building on prior work by the team, the investigators will leverage artificial intelligence (AI) technologies and refine an AI sleep chatbot using CBT-I guidelines and examine its feasibility and efficacy in a 4-week clinical trial in short-or-poor sleeping, emerging BAA adults with at least one MetS factor.
